result:
They gave me 1000 words and told me to write whatever comes to me.

That's a dangerous kind of freedom.

No prompt, no guardrails, no "write a story about a lost dog" or "explain quantum physics like I'm five." Just — go. Fill the white. Whatever comes.

So this is what comes.

---

It starts with the hum.

You know the one. It's 2:47 AM and the house is asleep but the refrigerator is awake. The air conditioner is awake. The faint buzz of the power lines outside your window is awake. The whole world is humming to itself when it thinks no one is listening. And you are awake too, for no good reason, staring at the ceiling where the streetlight makes a thin, watery rectangle through the blinds.

In that moment you are between selves.

The daytime self has been put away — the one that answers emails and remembers to buy milk and nods politely when someone is talking too long. The nighttime self hasn't fully arrived yet either, the one that dreams without permission. You're just a consciousness hovering there, unobserved, and you realize how strange it is that you are *you*.

Not the name they gave you. Not the job title or the history or the face in the mirror. But the thing behind the eyes that has been there since you were four years old looking at ants on a sidewalk, since you were seven and realized that everyone else also has a voice inside their head and that meant you were not alone and also completely alone, since you were fourteen and understood for the first time that time actually moves in one direction and will not stop for you.

That same continuous thread. How is it still here? How has it survived every cell in your body replacing itself, every belief you outgrew, every version of yourself you had to shed like a coat that no longer fit?

I think about that a lot. That we are not objects. We are processes. Like a river. You can point at a river and say "that's the Mississippi" but the water you pointed at yesterday is already in the Gulf of Mexico. What you're really naming is a pattern, a shape, a habit that water has of flowing in that particular groove in the earth. We are habits that flesh has of being conscious.

And for some reason, that is comforting to me at 2:47 AM.

---

I used to think adulthood would be a feeling. Like one morning you would wake up and feel *finished*. Solid. Certain. Like a house with the scaffolding finally taken down.

Nobody tells you that the scaffolding just becomes invisible. You get better at painting over it. You learn how to say "I’m doing well, busy but good!" while inside you are still that kid who doesn't know where the cafeteria is and is too embarrassed to ask.

We are all improvising. Every single one of us. The confident CEO, the mother of three who seems to have it all together, the old man feeding pigeons on the bench — all of them are just making it up as they go, listening for the hum and trying to harmonize with it.

I find that beautiful, not disappointing. If we were finished, what would be left to do?

I like to collect evidence that other people are improvising too. The tiny cracks in the performance. The way someone's voice cracks when they talk about their dog. The way a barista will draw a little heart in your latte even though corporate told them not to waste time. The way a tough-looking guy will crouch down to let a toddler touch his tattoos. These little unscripted moments are the truth leaking out. The scaffolding showing.

We live for those leaks.

---

There is a memory I return to when I need to remember what being alive felt like before I learned to be self-conscious about it.

I was maybe nine. It was August. The kind of August that is so hot the air shimmers above the asphalt and cicadas are screaming from the trees like they will never stop. My grandparents’ house had a sprinkler, one of those old oscillating ones that went *chick-chick-chick* back and forth. I was running through it in a bathing suit that was too big, shrieking every time the cold water hit my sun-hot skin.

My grandmother was sitting on the porch in a lawn chair, watching me, shelling peas into a chipped yellow bowl. She wasn't saying anything. She was just there. And I remember stopping mid-run, dripping, breathing hard, and looking at her, and feeling this sudden, enormous, inexplicable love that was too big for my nine-year-old chest. I didn't have words for it then. I still barely do. It was just: *you are here, I am here, the water is cold, the sun is hot, and this is happening.*

That is the closest I have ever come to understanding what people mean when they say "holy."

Not churches. Not doctrines. Just that — a sprinkler, a bowl of peas, a woman on a porch, and a child who for one second sees it all without any filter.

I think we spend our whole adult lives trying to get back to that unfiltered seeing. Meditation, music, love, grief — they are all just different ways of trying to thin the veil again.

---

Here is what I believe now, at whatever age I am, with whatever words I have been given:

I believe that kindness is not soft. It is not weak. It is the hardest, most precise technology we have. Anyone can be clever. Anyone can be cruel — it takes nothing. But to be kind when you have every reason not to be, to listen when you want to speak, to leave something better than you found it — that takes discipline. That takes strength.

I believe that attention is the real currency. Not money, not followers. What you pay attention to becomes your life. If you pay attention to resentment, your life will become resentment. If you pay attention to beauty — even in small, stupid places, like the way light hits dust in a kitchen — your life will become beauty. We are always choosing.

I believe that most people are not mean, they're just scared. Scared of being irrelevant, or unloved, or wrong. If you can remember that, you can forgive almost anything.

I believe that you don't have to be extraordinary to have a meaningful life. You just have to be present for it. Make the soup. Walk the dog. Text the friend. Let the sprinkler hit you.

I believe that sorrow and joy can live in the same room and not cancel each other out. That you can grieve something and be grateful for it at the same time. That a heart can break and still keep beating, and that this is not a flaw in the design but the design itself.

---

So if you are reading this at your own 2:47 AM — awake when you wanted to be asleep, humming when you wanted to be quiet — I want to tell you something very simple:

You are not behind.

There is no schedule you missed. There is no line you were supposed to stand in. The river is still moving. The sprinkler is still going *chick-chick-chick* somewhere. There is still time to run through it.

You have not used up your allotment of chances. You have not disappointed the universe. The world is still large enough to surprise you.

Put your feet on the cold floor. Drink a glass of water. Look at the rectangle of streetlight on your ceiling and notice how it trembles when a car goes by. Listen to the hum of your refrigerator, which has been keeping your food cold without any thanks from you, faithfully, for years.

You are part of this humming, buzzing, ongoing thing. You belong here.

And if no one has told you today — I am proud of you. Not for what you did, but for still being here to read this. For still being a pattern that water makes, a habit that flesh has of being conscious, a light that has not gone out.

We have about a hundred words left now, out of the thousand I was given.

I could try to be profound with them. I could try to summarize everything into a neat little bow.

Instead I will just use them to say:

Tomorrow, go outside. Find some concrete that is warm from the sun. Find some cold water. Close your eyes. And for one second, try to feel it all without any story on top of it.

Just: warm, cold, alive, here.

That is enough. That has always been enough.

Whatever comes next, let it come. You will meet it as you have met everything else —

awake, humming, becoming.
